Cross scenarios interpretable quantification of maintenance action effects on system health via liquid Kolmogorov–Arnold operator based framework
abstract: Predictive maintenance for safety–critical assets demands accurate forecasting and interpretable understanding of how maintenance actions affect system health across diverse regimes. We introduce a liquid Kolmogorov–Arnold operator (KAO)-based model that learns a physically grounded health indicator (HI) while revealing maintenance-driven degradation dynamics. The model comprises three components: (i) a BoltzmannKAN attention layer learning per-channel thresholds and temperatures to identify key sensors before and after maintenance; (ii) a self-organizing pool of interpretable operators representing distinct degradation modes, connected via liquid, temperature-controlled soft routing for smooth regime transitions; and (iii) unsupervised contrastive learning around maintenance events anchoring the HI without remaining useful life (RUL) labels, guided by a unified loss combining reconstruction, maintenance-quality classification, and regularization terms. The liquid-KAO framework generates a forward-looking HI reflecting both short-term recovery and long-term degradation moderation, while its autoregressive design enables post-maintenance forecasting and counterfactual analysis. On C-MAPSS with simulated interventions, it provides stable forecasts and identifies mechanism shifts consistent with injected actions; on the real-world National General Aviation Flight Information Database (NGAFID) aircraft maintenance dataset (14 maintenance classes), it achieves 0.84 accuracy, surpassing prior baselines with subsystem-level interpretability and HI-based reliability metrics. Overall, liquid-KAO unifies accuracy, transferability, and equation-level interpretability for reliable maintenance validation and scheduling.

Quantum Annealing approaches for Minimal Cut Set identification in fault trees
abstract: The identification of Minimal Cut Sets (MCS) in Fault Trees (FT) is central to Probabilistic Safety Assessment (PSA) but remains computationally challenging. While gate-based quantum algorithms have been explored, Quantum Annealing (QA) has not yet been applied to this industrial use case. This work investigates the application of QA to MCS identification by modeling the FT as a boolean function and implementing three existing SAT to Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) encoding strategies. We evaluate these encodings using generated 3-SAT instances as well as realistic FT benchmarks, and conduct experiments on a simulated annealer and two D-Wave architectures. Our results show that the encoding with reusable auxiliary variables is the most efficient in terms of qubit requirements and embedding scalability. In addition, the Zephyr architecture provides improved embeddability compared to Pegasus, reflected in reduced chain break occurrences and better performance on larger instances. Across these experiments, QA demonstrates the ability to sample diverse valid solutions, making it suitable for exploring the solution space of MCS problems. However, its performance remains limited by hardware constraints and the maximum number of possible shots, which prevent exhaustive identification of all solutions in larger instances.

Extending the robustness analysis of uncertain minimum spanning trees via upper set tolerances
abstract: Catastrophic disruptions—natural disasters, cyberattacks, and cascading failures—routinely compromise critical infrastructure networks, where even small simultaneous deteriorations across multiple links can rapidly render optimal spanning trees suboptimal. Classical single-edge tolerance analysis fails to capture such coordinated risk escalations. This paper introduces a new uncertainty-theory-based framework that extends single tolerances to set tolerances : the upper set tolerance (UST) quantifies the maximum total risk increase (distributed arbitrarily across a set of edges) that preserves the optimality of the current minimum spanning tree, while the dual upper set tolerance (DUST) identifies the minimal total increase sufficient to destroy it. We derive exact polynomial-time computation for DUST and tight polynomial-time bounds for UST, eliminating the need for repeated re-optimization. Applied to transportation and infrastructure networks under deep uncertainty, these metrics enable planners to identify critical edge groups, quantify systemic vulnerability, and design more resilient topologies. The framework bridges a long-standing gap between classical sensitivity analysis and modern belief-based uncertainty modeling in reliability engineering.

title: Physics-informed deep surrogate demand modeling for framed core-tube structures under seismic loadings
abstract: Nonlinear time-history analysis of high-rise framed core-tube structures is computationally intensive, particularly when repeated simulations are required for seismic performance evaluation. This study develops a physics-informed deep surrogate framework for rapid prediction of multi-component nonlinear seismic demands. A parameterized family of structural models is generated within practical geometric and material ranges, and nonlinear bidirectional analyses under 500 ground motions are conducted to construct a comprehensive training dataset. Four engineering demand parameters—inter-story drift, top displacement, top acceleration, and base shear—are predicted in a sequence-to-sequence manner. The influence of temporal sequence length on predictive performance and convergence behavior is systematically examined. The optimal configuration achieves test-set coefficients of determination exceeding 0.93–0.95 across all response components. To enhance physical consistency, a hybrid loss formulation incorporating aggregate constraints on peak response, energy balance, and Arias intensity is introduced. While global statistical accuracy remains comparable to purely data-driven models, the physics-informed formulation reduces physically meaningful errors and improves training stability. Once trained, the surrogate enables millisecond-level inference, offering substantial computational savings relative to nonlinear finite-element simulations within the defined structural and seismic parameter domains, and provides a computational basis for future fragility- and reliability-oriented applications.

The price of decentralization in managing engineering systems through multi-agent reinforcement learning
abstract: Inspection and maintenance (I&M) planning involves sequential decision making under uncertainties and incomplete information, and can be modeled as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP). While single-agent deep reinforcement learning provides approximate solutions to POMDPs, it does not scale well in multi-component systems. Scalability can be achieved through multi-agent deep reinforcement learning (MADRL), which decentralizes decision-making across multiple agents, locally controlling individual components. However, this decentralization can induce cooperation pathologies that degrade the optimality of the learned policies. To examine these effects in I&M planning, we introduce a set of deteriorating systems in which redundancy is varied systematically. These benchmark environments are designed such that computation of centralized (near-)optimal policies remains tractable, enabling direct comparison of solution methods. We implement and benchmark a broad set of MADRL algorithms spanning fully centralized and decentralized training paradigms, from value-factorization to actor-critic methods. Our results show a clear effect of redundancy on coordination: MADRL algorithms achieve near-optimal performance in series-like settings, whereas increasing redundancy amplifies coordination challenges and can lead to optimality losses. Nonetheless, decentralized agents learn structured policies that consistently outperform optimized heuristic baselines, highlighting both the promise and current limitations of decentralized learning for scalable maintenance planning.

Entropy Modelling of Hierarchical Structures and Systemic Risk
abstract: Hierarchical systems are usually complex, adaptive and have stochastic behavior. One of the pressing issues in the field of reliability of such systems is the problem of systemic risks, which refer to the risk of failure of the entire system, rather than simply the failure of its individual parts. Currently, systemic risk research is understudied, and adequate tools for its analysis and detection have yet to be developed. In this article, regarding hierarchical systems, we propose using the differential entropy of continuous random vectors, which is a fundamental characteristic of any system with stochastic behavior, as a tool for studying systemic risk. The entropy of a random vector is decomposed into two components, one of which characterizes chaos, and the other characterizes the interdependence between its elements. An interpretation of systemic risk in terms of entropy measures of randomness and dependence is given. All the main variants of correlation relationships in hierarchical systems are considered, including cross correlation between all elements, between subsystems at different levels of the system, and between one element and a group of elements. The simplicity of the analytical formulas allows for the practical application of the vector entropy model. Moreover, the proposed approach provides the opportunity of monitoring not only the entire system, but also its individual subsystems, which expands the possibilities of its practical use. Examples of Gaussian hierarchical systems are given, which demonstrate the possibility of using the entropy model for monitoring systemic risk.
